described in your "Part 2" response, explaining how they could participate 
to a "significant extent" in a similar future project. 
 
4. We are interested in responding to the AEDC Velocity Consortium Call for White Papers but have 
a question about the partnership requirements. The company that I work for already qualifies as a 
small business.  Because we qualify as a small business do we still need to partner with another 
small business, university, or National Laboratory to meet this requirement? 
a. Thank you for your question. This is an excellent point of clarification as it highlights a 
unique scenario for a prime contractor that is already a small business. 
 
The direct answer is:  Yes, even as a small business, your company is still required to 
identify at least one partner company in your whitepaper response to satisfy the "Part 4: 
Innovation and Partnership Capability" requirement. 
 
Here is the detailed rationale to guide your submission: 
 
1. The Purpose of the Requirement: Demonstrating Partnership Capability 
The primary purpose of the Part 4 requirement is not just to verify a company's status; it is 
to evaluate a prospective member's  capability to form innovative partnerships.  The 
Government needs to see that every member of the Alliance, regardless of their own size 
or status, has the ability to "reach back" and build effective teams with other specialized 
companies. This ensures a dynamic and collaborative industrial base for all future projects. 
 
Therefore, simply stating that your own company is a small business, while valuable, 
does not demonstrate this crucial partnership capability. 
 
2. How to Meet the Requirement as a Small Business 
Your status as a small business gives you two clear and powerful paths to satisfy this 
requirement in your whitepaper. You must show how you would form a team that satisfies 
one of the following conditions: 
 
Option A: Partner with a Non-Traditional Defense Contractor (NDC) or Nonprofit 
Research Institution. 

• In your whitepaper, you would identify an NDC or a Nonprofit Research 
Institution. 
• You would then explain how this partnership would satisfy condition (A) of the 
statute ("at least one nontraditional defense contractor...participating to a 
significant extent"). 
• This is a very strong approach as it demonstrates your ability to bring in partners 
with a different status than your own. 
 
Option B: Partner with another Small Business. 
• In your whitepaper, you would identify another small business as your partner. 
• You would then explain how this partnership would satisfy condition (B) of the 
statute ("All significant participants...are small businesses"). 
• This is also a perfectly valid approach that demonstrates your ability to build 
teams within the small business community. 
 
3. Your Path Forward 
For your whitepaper submission, you should: 
• Choose one of the two options above. 
• Select a specific partner company (an NDC, a university, or another small 
business) that you have an existing relationship with. 
• In your "Part 4" response, provide the partner's name and CAGE code. 
• Crucially, link that partner's capabilities to the technical project you described in 
your "Part 2" response, explaining how you would work together and how their 
participation would be "significant." 
 
In summary, the requirement is less about what your company is and more about what your 
company can do in terms of building strong, compliant teams. We look forward to seeing 
your submission. 
 
5. Is it the Government's intent to issue future Velocity Alliance solicitations to all consortium 
members regardless of SOO type?  In other words, does the Government intend to in any way 
filter or limit solicitations consortium members will see based on our demonstrated competencies 
during the onboarding phase? 
a. The direct answer is: Yes, it is absolutely the Government's intent to issue all Project 
Opportunity Announcements (POAs) to all consortium members, regardless of the 
project's SOO type. 
 
Here is a more detailed explanation of the process and rationale: 
 
1. Fair and Open Opportunity for All Members 
The fundamental principle of the Alliance is to create a fair, competitive ecosystem among 
a pre-qualified pool of vendors. The Government will not filter or limit the distribution of 
POAs based on the competencies you demonstrated during the onboarding phase. 
 
When you are accepted into the Alliance, you are accepted into the entire enterprise. You 
will have full visibility on every single project opportunity, from "General Construction" 
to "Utilities," and everything in between. 

 
2. The Onboarding Phase vs. the Project Competition Phase 
It is helpful to think of this as a two-stage process: 
 
• Onboarding Phase (The "Entry Gate"): The purpose of your whitepaper, including 
your response to the technical questions, is to prove you have the minimum 
required technical competence and partnership capability to be a member of the 
Alliance. It is your ticket to get in the door. 
 
• Project Competition Phase (The "Performance Arena"): Once you are a member, 
it is then your business decision to determine which specific Project Opportunity 
Announcements (POAs) you wish to pursue. You are responsible for assessing 
your company's strengths, capabilities, and capacity to decide whether to submit a 
proposal for a given project. 
 
3. The Vendor's Responsibility 
The Government's responsibility is to ensure every member sees every opportunity. The 
member's responsibility is to "know your company"—to analyze each POA and make a 
smart business decision about whether their team has the right qualifications to submit a 
competitive proposal for that specific scope of work. 
 
In summary, we will not be creating sub -pools or specialized lists. All members will see 
all opportunities, ensuring a level playing field for every project competed under the AEDC 
Velocity Alliance. 
 
6. Once the consortium is established, does the Government intend to use white papers or similar 
means to down-select qualified performers for a given requirement/solicitation? 
a. The Government's primary goal is to use the most efficient and effective means to select 
a performer for each project. While a single-step proposal process is often the most 
streamlined approach, the specific competitive procedure will be tailored to the unique 
needs of each requirement. 
 
Project Opportunity Announcements (POAs) could be down-selected utilizing a variety 
of methods. These may include, but are not limited to: 
 
• Whitepapers 
• Full-blown Prototype Proposals 
• Oral Presentations 
• Or any other means the Government determines to fit that particular POA. 
 
The specific competitive procedure, including the format of the required response and the 
evaluation criteria, will be clearly defined within the POA for each project. 
 
This approach provides the Government with the necessary flexibility to structure each 
competition in a way that best ensures a successful outcome, while also providing a clear 
and fair opportunity for all Alliance members to participate.

Sources Sought/Request For Information (RFI) 
Education Platform Requirements 
1. Purpose and Scope 
 
This Sources Sought/ Request for Information is issued solely for market research and 
acquisition planning purposes. This notice does not constitute a Request for Quote (RFQ), 
Invitation for Bid (IFB), or Request for Proposal (RFP) and does not obligate the Government to 
issue a solicitation or make an award. 
 
Responses are voluntary. No reimbursement will be provided for costs associated with 
responding to this notice. 
 
The Department of War Education Activity (DoWEA) seeks information to better understand 
current industry capabilities, architectural approaches, data strategies, and maturity related to a 
single, cohesive enterprise education platform that supports DoWEA’s global Pre-K – 12 
mission. 
2. Background and Objective 
 
DoWEA operates a globally distributed education environment supporting instructional delivery, 
student services, and enterprise operations. As part of long-term modernization and consolidation 
planning, DoWEA is conducting market research to assess platforms that can: 
 
• Unify instructional and enterprise systems on a shared or tightly integrated data 
foundation. 
• Reduce system fragmentation and manual data movement. 
• Enable secure, near-real-time reporting, analytics, and AI-enabled insights at global scale. 
• Support interoperability with external analytics platforms and DoWEA-managed data 
environments. 
3. Teaching, Learning & Student Systems 
 
3.1 Integrated Platform Approach 
 
DoWEA is interested in platforms that support tightly integrated, natively developed or fully 
supported modules operating on a shared identity and data framework. Vendors may describe 
point to point or loosely coupled integrations; however, such approaches should be clearly 
identified and explained. 
3.2 Student Information System (SIS) 

2  
DoWEA seeks information on Student Information Systems (SIS) that can serve as the primary 
system of record for managing student data across the full student lifecycle. Areas of interest 
include, but are not limited to: 
 
• Enrollment, registration, scheduling, attendance, grading, gradebook management, 
transcripts, discipline/behavior tracking, and program participation. 
• Secure student records management with rolebased access control, audit logging, 
alignment with the Privacy Act of 1974 and applicable DoW privacy regulations, and 
configurable data retention rules. 
• Support for DoWEA specific calendars, grading policies, credits, and reporting 
requirements. 
• Standards based, documented APIs that support data import and export for students, 
enrollment, roster, attendance, grades, transcripts, behavior, and program status data, 
including near real time exchange where available. 
3.3 Learning Management System (LMS) – Optional Module with Mandatory 
Integration 
 
DoWEA seeks information on education platforms that either include a native LMS module or 
provide strong, production ready integration with commonly used third party LMS solutions (for 
example, Schoology and Google Classroom) but not limited to those solutions. Areas of interest 
include the platform’s ability to support: 
 
• Seamlessly integrate with external LMS platforms using standards-based mechanisms 
(e.g., LTI 1.3/Advantage, OneRoster, and secure APIs). 
• Support automated provisioning and synchronization of: 
o Courses, sections, teachers, students, and roles. 
o Assignments and grading workflows. 
o Enrollment changes, schedule updates, and staff reassignments. 
• Enable bidirectional grade pass back so that instructional grading performed in the LMS 
flows reliably to the SIS gradebook and transcript processes. 
• Maintain consistent user identity, authentication (SSO), and role-based access across the 
SIS and integrated LMS environments. 
• Provide visibility for instructional activity and learning signals (e.g., assignment 
completion, engagement indicators) for reporting and analytics, regardless of whether 
instruction occurs in a native or third-party LMS. 
• Ensure mobile support and parity of experience where supported by the external LMS. 
If a native LMS module is offered, vendors may describe capabilities related to: 
• Course and content management, assignments, rubrics, discussions, collaboration tools, 
and mobile applications. 
• Standards-based grading aligned with SIS grade calculation and transcript workflows. 

3  
• Learning analytics focused on engagement, progress, pacing, mastery, and course 
completion. 
 
3.4 Assessment 
 
DoWEA seeks information on assessment capabilities that support formative, benchmark, and 
summative use cases. Areas of interest include: 
 
• Centralized, reusable item banks with tagging, version control, and alignment to 
standards. 
• Accommodation management aligned to IEP/504 requirements and multilingual learner 
needs. 
• Secure test administration with support for offline or low-bandwidth operation in global 
environments. 
• Proctoring and academic integrity safeguards, as applicable. 
• Import/export APIs supporting assessment results, accommodations, and item metadata. 
• Integration with LMS platforms (native or third-party) for assignment-based and 
classroom-embedded assessments. 
 
3.5 Special Education and Student Support Programs 
 
DoWEA seeks information on platforms that support special education and student services 
workflows. Areas of interest include support for: 
 
• IEP/504, Multilingual Learner Programs (MLP), Advanced Academic Programs (AAP), 
and MTSS/RTI frameworks. 
• Intervention planning, service delivery logging, progress monitoring, and compliance 
reporting. 
• Strict role-based privacy controls to safeguard sensitive student data. 
• Standards-based APIs supporting exchange of accommodations, service records, progress 
data, and compliance indicators. 
 
4. Reporting, Analytics, and Data Interoperability 
 
DoWEA is interested in understanding how platforms support reporting and analytics across 
instructional and enterprise domains. Areas of interest include: 
 
• Real-time or near real-time reporting across SIS, Assessment, Special Programs, and 
LMS platforms (native or third-party). 
• Role-appropriate dashboards for teachers, school leaders, district/regional leadership, and 
headquarters personnel. 
• Reporting shall not be degraded or functionally limited using an external LMS. 

4  
Vendors should describe how reporting data is structured and made available for analytical and 
AI use cases. 
 
5. Enterprise Operations & Business Services 
 
DoWEA seeks information on enterprise education platforms that provide or integrate with 
operational and business services to support a global education environment. The following 
areas represent capabilities of interest for market research purposes. 
 
5.1 Finance / ERP 
 
Areas of interest include: 
 
• General Ledger, Accounts Payable/Receivable, multi-fund accounting, grants 
management, budgeting and forecasting. 
• Procurement and eProcurement workflows. 
• Inventory management and school activity funds. 
• Auditability and reporting are suitable for federal oversight. 
 
5.2 Human Resources /Human Capital Management (HCM) 
Areas of interest include: 
• Manpower management, including position control, Staff Deployment (by school, 
program, or funding source), Trend and Forecasting (enrollment driven staffing models), 
and Scenario Planning and Forecasting. 
• Recruiting, onboarding, licensure and credential tracking, staff evaluations, and substitute 
management. 
• Alignment of staff roles and credentials with instructional and system access. 
• Integration with enterprise identity and access management systems. 
 
5.3 Facilities /Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) 
Areas of interest include: 
• Work order management, preventive maintenance scheduling, asset lifecycle tracking, 
and space utilization. 
• Safety, security, and facilities related compliance workflows. 
 
5.4 Transportation 
Areas of interest include: 
• Route planning, ridership management, and parent notifications. 

5  
• Fleet management and vehicle maintenance tracking. 
 
5.5 IT Service Management (ITSM) & End-User Computing 
Areas of interest include: 
• Device, software, and asset management. 
• IT ticketing and service workflows. 
• Integration with Unified Endpoint Management (UEM/MDM) platforms. 
• Classroom device management and instructional visibility. 
 
6. Unified Data, Analytics & Interoperability 
 
6.1 Unified Data Architecture 
 
DoWEA seeks information on platform support unified or federated data approaches across 
instructional and enterprise domains. Areas of interest include: 
 
• A shared or tightly federated data model across SIS, LMS, ERP, HR, facilities, 
transportation, and IT operations. 
• Near real-time data flows with minimal manual reconciliation. 
 
6.2 APIs & Interoperability Standards 
 
Vendors may describe support for open APIs and industry standards, including: 
 
• Open REST APIs with pagination, filtering, and webhook/event support. 
• Support for current and future standards, including but not limited to: 
o IMS OneRoster 1.1+ 
o Ed-Fi Data Standard 4.0+ (native or certified adapter) 
o LTI 1.3/Advantage 
o QTI/APIP (as applicable) 
o SCORM (legacy) and xAPI 
o Identity standards: SAML 2.0, OIDC/OAuth 2.0, SCIM 2.0 
 
6.3 AI-Enabled Analytics & Business Intelligence 
 
DoWEA is interested in understanding how platforms support analytics and AI enabled insights 
across instructional and operational domains. Areas of interest include: 
 
• Executive, instructional, and operational dashboards. 
• Early warning indicators for attendance, grades, behavior, and course completion with 
configurable thresholds. 

6  
• Machine learning explainability, including feature importance and counterfactual 
explanations. 
• Intervention tracking linked to analytic triggers. 
• Self-service analytics, including natural language queries where appropriate. 
• Export or integration with DoWEA managed data warehouse or lakehouse infrastructure. 
• Availability of Metadata catalogs with data lineage visualization. 
 
7.  Data Quality & Master Data Management 
Areas of interest include: 
• Automated validation for completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and consistency. 
• Pre-configured quality checks for critical data (student demographics, attendance, grades, 
staff credentials). 
• Data quality dashboards, alerts, and trend analysis. 
• Support for DoWEA defined custom validation rules. 
• Master Data Management for students, staff, schools, and courses. 
• Data classification, PII tagging. and retention/minimization controls. 
 
8. Reporting Integration with External AI-Enabled Analytics Platforms (e.g., MS Fabric) 
 
DoWEA seeks information on how platform reporting and analytics capabilities interoperate 
seamlessly with external, AI enabled enterprise analytics platforms, including but not limited to 
MS Fabric, Power BI, and DoWEA managed data warehouse or lakehouse environments. The 
reporting architecture must support both native platform reporting and advanced external 
analytics without data duplication, vendor lock-in, or loss of data fidelity. Vendors shall 
describe how their solutions enable secure, scalable, and transparent integration across 
instructional, operational, and enterprise analytics environments. 
9. Data Access & Export 
 
The platform shall provide secure, documented, and supported mechanisms to expose 
reporting data to external AI-enabled analytics platforms, including: 
 
o REST-based APIs. 
o Event- or change-based data feeds. 
o Bulk and incremental data export capabilities for historical and snapshot data. 
• Data access methods shall support near real-time and scheduled delivery patterns suitable 
for ingestion by AI-enabled analytics platforms. 
• Exported data shall be available in open, analytics-optimized formats, including but not 
limited to: 
o Parquet 
o Delta 

7  
o CSV 
o JSON 
• The solution shall not require proprietary or vendor-locked connectors to integrate with 
MS Fabric or comparable AI-enabled analytic platforms. 
 
10. Compatibility with AI-Enabled Analytics Architectures 
 
The reporting capability shall be compatible with modern analytics and AI architecture, 
including: 
 
• Lakehouse and warehouse ingestion models, enabling reporting data to land directly in 
DoWEA-managed analytic environments. 
• Semantic and analytical models that support downstream BI, AI, and machine learning 
workloads without reengineering. 
• Data pipelines, notebooks, and AI workflows, enabling DoWEA to apply advanced 
analytics, machine learning, and cross-domain insights beyond the platform’s native 
capabilities. 
Vendors shall clearly describe: 
 
• How reporting data is structured for analytical and AI consumption. 
• How data supports instructional, operational, and enterprise analytics use cases. 
• How platform data can be joined with non-platform data sources (e.g., finance, HR, 
logistics, cybersecurity, or operations data) in external analytics environments. 
 
11. Data Model Transparency & Metadata 
 
The vendor must provide full transparency of the reporting data model, including: 
 
o Tables, fields, relationships, and keys. 
o Business definitions for metrics, indicators, and calculated values. 
• A metadata catalog shall be available natively or exportable, supporting: 
o Schema discovery. 
o Data lineage from source systems through reporting outputs. 
o Field-level descriptions suitable for ingestion into enterprise metadata catalogs. 
• Any native semantic layers must be exportable, reproducible, or documentable for use in 
external AI-enabled analytic platforms. 
 
12. Security, Governance & Access Control 
 
Reporting interfaces shall comply with DoWEA security and data governance requirements, 
including: 

8  
o Role-based access controls aligned to SIS, HR, and enterprise roles. 
o Row-level and column-level security enforcement that is preserved or enforceable 
in external platforms. 
 
The solution shall support enterprise identity integration to enable: 
 
o Consistent authentication and authorization across the platform and external 
analytics environments. 
o Centralized logging and auditability. 
 
Data classification, PII tagging, retention, and minimization controls shall be preserved when 
reporting data is exposed to or consumed by AI-enabled analytic platforms. 
 
13. Incremental, Event-Driven & Near Real-Time Reporting 
 
The platform shall support incremental data extraction (e.g., change data capture or equivalent) 
to reduce latency and processing overhead. Event driven updates via webhooks or event streams 
consumable by AI enabled platforms. 
 
• Examples include but are not limited to: 
o Enrollment changes, 
o Attendance updates, 
o Grade postings, 
o Intervention changes, 
o IEP status updates.

### Sheet: Experience
PBES RFI - Experience
Questions
What experience, if any, do you have with supporting the Department of Air Force (DAF) Planning, Programming, and Budgeting (PPB) processes--both MAJCOM and Air Staff?  Please provide examples.
Describe your experience and internal process for creating system training materials.  Based on your familiarity with PBES what are your recomendations to implement changes and improvements to the current training material.
Describe your level of experience and/or any certifications held with each the following: Enterprise Performance Management (EPM), Oracle Analytics Server (OAS), Oracle DB Server, Oracle Data Integrator (ODI), Oracle DRM, Oracle HTTP Server (OHS), Oracle Hyperion Planning, Essbase, Oracle Internet Directory, Oracle Weblogic Server, RHEL, Windows Server 2019 and newer.   If so, please describe how those experiences would be used to support PBES and it's mission to generate Program Objective Memorandum, Budget Estimate Submissin, Rapid Allocation Process, and President's Budget seamlessly. Describe your specific experience managing and configuring Oracle DRM or a similar Master Data Management (MDM) tool within a federal financial context. How do you ensure data governance and stewardship?
Describe your experience in developing, maintaining, and troubleshooting automated data interfaces between a primary system like PBES and external authoritative data sources. Please provide an example where you successfully automated an interface that was previously a manual process.
Please provide contract number, name of customer/organization supported, customer/organization POC including contact information for the questions listed above, if applicable.

### Sheet: Staffing
PBES RFI - Staffing
Questions
What certifications or qualifications would you recommend your staff hold in areas such as software development, cybersecurity, database/system administration, or project management? Do you currently have personnel with the recommended certifications and qualifications to work PBES should they receive authorization to do so?
PBES is hosted on the SIPR network; can you provide a capability support team that has the appropriate security clearances and IA (IAT II or higher) Workforce Certifications to sustain a classified system?
Do you currently have Functional Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) on staff? Functional SME’s must be experts with the POM (Program Ojective Memorandum) , BES (Budget Estimate Submission) and PB (President's Budget) processes from Major Command level to Office of Secretary of Defense.  This includes the Programming function with the different AF panels through the Appropriation Managers on the Budget side of the process. The SMEs must also be familiar with the entire PPB&E process and how it all ties together.  They must be able to integrate the 30-year Plan with the Programming and Budget FYDP (Five Year Defense Plan).
Please provide contract number, name of customer/organization supported, customer/organiztion POC including contact information for the questions listed above, if applicable.

### Sheet: Management
PBES RFI - Management
Questions
Can you describe the recommended team structure, including roles (e.g., system analysts, software engineers, database administrators)?  Can you describe how your team would collaborate with the functional customer (e.g. a Functional Management Office (FMO)) and the Program Management Office (PMO) to ensure seamless POM, BES, PB development?
How would you plan to allocate staff resources for a POM/PB project?  Can you provide details on staffing levels, including full-time equivalents (FTEs) and any subcontractors?  What contingency plans would you put in place to address unexpected staff shortages or turnover?
How would your company handle data validation for rounds (versions within the cycle that add rates, manpower, DAF decisions)  during budget cycles? What steps would you take to update financial or performance data? How would you manage changes and ensure consistency in the data?
Describe your management approach for supporting cybersecurity readiness and providing software ugrades to PBES while delivering new capabiilty and keeping PBES operational (minimum downtime).
How would you manage the project timeline, milestones, and deliverables?  What communication channels would you use to keep the Government informed of your progress and to address any issues?  How would you manage risk and how would you share those risks with the FMO and PMO?
How would you handle changes to requirements, scope, or priorities during the project? Outline your change management process.  What mechanisms would you use to communicate changes to the Government?
Describe your approach to quality assurance (QA) and testing. How would you verify the accuracy and reliability of the IT system the DAF uses to generate a POM and PB?  What testing methodologies (e.g., unit testing, integration testing) would your team employ?
This customer operates under very stringent timelines.  What project management tools and techniques do you use to ensure timely and within-budget delivery?
Regarding standing up/building development environments, what  critical milestones or phases would you include in a schedule or timeline? How would you account for potential delays or unforeseen challenges?  What resources (human and technical) would you allocate to meet the timeline? On average, what is the timeline to build a development environment?
The Government will provide a development environment (DevLab). Describe your experience working within a Government-Furnished Environment. How do you manage configurations, dependencies, and documentation when you do not control the underlying infrastructure?
Please provide contract number, name of customer/organization supported, customer/organiztion POC including contact information for the questions listed above, if applicable.

### Sheet: Processes
PBES RFI - Processes
Questions
Would you provide training to government personnel on using the IT system for POM and PB generation?  How would you transfer knowledge and documentation to ensure long-term sustainability?
Describe how you would align domain subject matter expertise with leading technologies to drive transformation for DAF financial planning/financial management information systems—specifically program and budgeting systems—while leveraging leading commercial software and best practices.
How would your company ensure accurate and reliable data within the annual PPB (POM, RAP, BES, PB) process?  What validation rules or procedures would you follow to verify data integrity?  Are there any specific tools or methodologies you would employ for data validation?  Are there opportunities to leverage BOTS or other automated technology for accelerating data validation exercises?
Provide examples of risks encountered in previous similar projects and how you managed them to ensure project success.
How would you deliver—using Agile, CI/CD, DevSecOps processes—new capabilities for approved requirements while addressing/reducing significant technical debt in a Cloud One environment?
How would you provide "over the shoulder" support to PBES end users in the Pentagon to include supporting with data loading, data validation, use of PBES, etc?
Describe the process you would use to support the PBES PMO/FMO with requirements development, requirements prioritization, product backlog refinement, program increment planning, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospectives, leadership reviews, demonstrations, technical interchanges and engineering reviews.
Tell us about your PPBE experience and experience with systems that supports that process.  Expand how you would validate accuracy and support the system workflow processes and procedures.
What processes would you use in PBES to support Financial and Program Structures such as PE numbers, appropriate codes, program codes, operating agency codes, weapon system codes, program activity codes, and J-books?
Beyond general quality assurance, what is your specific approach to performance and load testing, particularly in preparation for peak usage during critical POM/BES/PB budget cycles? Describe the tools and metrics you would use to ensure the system remains stable and responsive under stress.
Please provide contract number, name of customer/organization supported, customer/organiztion POC including contact information for the questions listed above, if applicable.

The Air Force Materiel Command (AFMC), Air Force Life Cycle Management Center 
(AFLCMC) Business and Enterprise Systems Directorate (BES) Financial Systems Division 
(GBG) Contracting Division (GBK), Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (WPAFB), Ohio is 
conducting market research seeking vendor configuration and capabilities for support, operation, 
maintenance and enhancement of the Program and Budget Enterprise System (PBES). 
 
This RFI is for planning purposes only and shall not be considered as an invitation for bid, 
request for quotation, request for proposal (RFP), or as an obligation on the part of the 
Government to acquire any products or services. Your response to this RFI will be treated as 
information only. No entitlement to payment of direct or indirect costs or charges by the 
Government will arise as a result of contractor submission of responses to this announcement or 
the Government use of such information. This request does not constitute a solicitation for 
proposals or the authority to enter into negotiations to award a contract. No funds have been 
authorized, appropriated, or received for this effort. 
 
The information provided is considered market research and may be used by the Department Air 
Force (DAF) in developing its acquisition strategy, Statement of Objectives (SOO) or

responsible for adequately marking proprietary or competition sensitive information contained in

accurate, and timely financial information in support of program budget and resource allocation 
decisions. 
 
The Air Force Program Executive Office (AFPEO) Business Enterprise Systems (BES) 
Financial Systems Division (GBG) is responsible for performing and managing the acquisition, 
development, implementation, capability support, and life cycle management in support of 
PBES.  Electronic reporting for the planning, programming, and budgeting (PPB) process makes 

PBES a vital component of the Air Force community’s effort to provide timely and accurate 
budget information to make Congressional decisions.

support to provide software configuration, capability support, and user support for PBES and its 
users. As it pertains to software configuration, the contractor shall take an iterative approach to 
ensure feedback can be acted on quickly and that responsive changes can be made at each stage 
of a sprint or product cycle. 
 
The Contractor shall also support the PMO and the SAF/FMIB’s FMO’s (Functional 
Management Office) continuous improvement of the PBES solution throughout the PBES 
lifecycle. The Contractor shall support the PMO and FMO’s management of business capability, 
technical implementation, and configuration for PBES, including continued cybersecurity 
readiness and enduring support for, and required upgrades to, PBES. All design 
methodology/decisions for the environments/application shall be approved by the PMO and 
SAF/FMIB FMO prior to implementation. 
 
The Contractor shall utilize the Agile framework and associated processes documented by the 
PMO to perform development and support sustainment activities for PBES as an entire system, 
to include its various components and all underlying prerequisites. Activities and components 
include, but are not limited to: transition, planning, requirements definition, capability 
development, defect resolution, enhancement development, code refactoring, program increment 
planning and execution, integration and design, configuration management, testing (both 
automated and manual), demonstrations, cybersecurity, training, architecture management, 
database development, management and architecture, data validation, data modeling, data 
extract, transform and load development and processes, environment management, system 
operations support, problem reports and resolutions, standards compliance, data deliverables, 
intellectual property management and compliance, and government furnished property 
management. These activities require the Contractor to be involved in enterprise level strategy 
and planning for PBES, architectural and solution engineering and management, business 
systems compliance and management, agile team iteration planning and execution, and user 
interface and training. USAF owns and operates PBES, and as such is an integrated stakeholder 
and team member of all Contractor activities related to PBES. Likewise, the Contractor is an 
integrated team member of all PBES planning, development, testing, and operations and support. 
 
PBES requires customer service focused on the user experience and technical support focused on

1 | P a g e  
 
 
REQUEST FOR INFORMATION 
 
AGENCY: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Customs and Border Protection 
Office of Field Operations, Non-Intrusive Inspection Program 
 
 
TITLE: Artificial Intelligence for Image Adjudication   ISSUANCE DATE: April 30, 2026 
 
THIS IS A REQUEST FOR INFORMATION (RFI) ONLY. This RFI is issued solely for information 
and planning purposes; it does not constitute a Request for Proposal (RFP) nor a promise to issue an 
RFP or other solicitation. Furthermore, those who respond to this RFI should not anticipate feedback 
about its submission, other than acknowledgment of receipt. This RFI does not commit the 
Government to contract for any supply or service. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) 
Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is not seeking proposals at this time. Respondents are advised 
that the U.S. Government will not pay any cost incurred in response to this RFI. All costs associated 
with responding to this RFI will be solely at the expense of the respondent. Not responding to this 
RFI does not preclude participation in any future solicitation. The information provided in this RFI is 
subject to change and is not binding on the Government. All submissions become the property of the 
Federal Government and will not be returned.  
 
1.0 Background 
CBP utilizes a suite of technology, techniques, and tactics as part of its multi-layered approach to 
meet the agency’s enduring mission priorities. Non-Intrusive Inspection (NII) systems are an integral 
part of CBP multi-layered enforcement strategy to assist personnel in examining cargo, baggage, and 
conveyances for illicit merchandise and substances without physically opening or unloading 
them. NII systems allow CBP to detect anomalies and materials that could pose potential threats to 
the U.S. economy and national security, while maintaining the flow of lawful trade and travel. NII 
systems include, but are not limited to, low and multi-energy X-ray portals (LEPs and MEPs), 
radiation portal monitors (RPMs), and chemical detectors. NII technology is currently deployed to 
airports, seaports, international mail facilities, express consignment, rail crossings, and land border 
ports of entry (POEs). 
For this RFI, CBP is specifically focused on large-scale (LS) imaging systems used to scan privately 
owned vehicles (POVs) and cargo vehicles (e.g. commercial trucks and similar conveyances). These 
systems generate high volumes of X-ray image data and associated metadata. Many large-scale image 
systems support the World Customs Organization (WCO) Unified File Format (UFF) as the accepted 
standard for packaging and sharing image data and metadata. CBP recognizes, however, that not all 
historical or legacy data will conform to WCO UFF, and that metadata fields may be incomplete, 
inconsistent, or inaccurate across locations, times, and OEMs. 
CBP is expanding the coverage of NII scanning technology with modern, integrated systems capable 
of greatly increasing scanning throughput. The volume of data generated by increased scanning 

 
2 | P a g e  
 
 
necessitates innovative solutions to maintain efficiency and effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
and Machine Learning (ML) models can be leveraged as tools to assist CBP employees with making 
better decisions faster, reviewing and synthesizing data, improving efficiency and learning from every 
new piece of information. Over the next few years, CBP plans to incorporate AI/ML tools into NII 
and other CBP processes, explore and test AI/ML use cases, and monitor advancements to AI/ML 
tools worldwide.  
CBP is seeking AI/ML tools to assist in NII image adjudication, to include anomaly detection, using a 
human-in-the-loop approach to ensure model integrity. It is important to note that CBP’s frontline 
personnel remain the most critical asset to thwarting illicit goods crossing our borders. AI/ML serves 
as a tool. A key goal of AI/ML use is to reduce the average NII examination processing time to 
achieve: (1) an increase in the number of cargo conveyances, private vehicles, packages, containers, 
and individuals scanned, (2) improved security, and (3) a reduction in the number of officer / agent 
hours used to conduct NII examinations – all without impact to the flow of legitimate trade and travel. 
While CBP’s most valued resource is its employees, CBP recognizes that technology is a vital 
element to mission success. CBP believes AI/ML tools will revolutionize border security and the flow 
of trade by seamlessly integrating NII systems and processes with relevant algorithms and other tools 
that will enable proactive threat detection, optimize resource allocation and ensure the swift and 
secure flow of commerce.  
2.0 AI/ML Goals and Objectives 
CBP seeks to incrementally implement AI/ML models that provide computer-assisted analysis of NII 
images and other data to increase the effectiveness and efficiency of NII operations. The AI/ML goals 
and objectives include: 
1. Incrementally implement AI/ML models that provide computer-assisted analysis of NII 
images and other data to increase the effectiveness and efficiency of NII operations, with an 
emphasis on very high daily volumes of LS‑NII scans of POVs and cargo vehicles. 
2. CBP is not seeking proposals whose primary deliverable is a proprietary data platform, data pipeline, 
or case management system. CBP anticipates using existing and planned CBP-owned data platforms, 
pipelines, and viewers, and seeks algorithmic components that can be integrated into that environment.  
3. Determine if AI/ML models can provide automated identification of anomalies, identification 
of conveyance modifications, manifest validation, contraband and narcotic identification, 
identification/verification of commodities or some combination of these capabilities through a 
series of algorithms applied to LS NII imagery and metadata. 
4. Use AI/ML models to assist officer image analysis on higher-risk shipments, identify higher-
risk areas of interest, and support a cost-effective, efficient operation. 
CBP recognizes that human performance is difficult to quantify, varies by context, and may not lend 
itself to a single benchmark. Metrics and evaluation approaches will need to be tailored to specific 
algorithms, roles, and operational needs. 

 
3 | P a g e  
 
 
3.0 Purpose of this RFI 
 
Through this RFI, CBP is seeking information from industry on how to best develop AI/ML models 
in concert with existing integrated NII system deployments, implementation of new X-ray scanning 
concepts of operation (CONOPs), and in response to current and anticipated future threats.  
 
CBP is particularly interested in modular algorithms and models that: 
• Operate on large scale NII imagery and associated metadata from POV and cargo vehicle 
scanners (with emphasis on WCO UFF where available); 
• Can be adapted to CBP operational needs and constraints; and 
• Can be integrated as drop-in components within existing CBP architectures, rather than 
requiring CBP to acquire or license new proprietary data platforms or data pipelines. 
 
CBP does not wish to constrain developers’ imaginations with a fixed set of use cases. The examples 
below are illustrative. At the same time, CBP must temper expectations regarding uniformity, 
completeness, and reliability of metadata, and the ability to define universal human performance 
baselines 
 
Vendors should address the following questions in their RFI response (tailored to large scale NII 
POV and cargo vehicle imagery and associated metadata): 
 
1. Describe algorithm products that you have developed, or are developing, for the following or 
related applications, including associated performance metrics: 
a. Anomaly detection 
b. Manifest / commodity verification 
c. Conveyance modification detection (concealment locations, etc.) 
d. Contraband detection (narcotics, weapons, currency, organic powders vs. organic 
goods) 
2. Describe your development approach and any key limitations, including: 
a. Types of models/architectures used and how they generalize across different ports, 
sensors, and operating conditions 
b. Known limitations, sensitivities, or failure modes relevant to LS-NII POV and cargo 
vehicle imagery 
3. Describe your capabilities on breaking down conveyance into components regions 
(segmentation). How does this support the applications described above? 
4. Is your algorithm image-type dependent (jpg, tiff, png, proprietary LS-NII X-ray formats, 
etc.)? Please describe supported image formats, including any current or planned support for 
UFF and how your solution ingests and uses UFF image data and metadata. 
5. Are there technical dependencies with your algorithm (system requirements)? Please describe 
require or recommended hardware, operating systems, and software dependencies for 
deployment at scale in CBP environments, particularly in cloud-based architectures. 

 
4 | P a g e  
 
 
6. Are there any technical incompatibilities? Particularly with industry accepted technologies 
(e.g., Windows vs Linux, Java vs .net, etc.). Please explain.  
7. What does a typical architecture look like? In other words, what key technologies are 
required, and how would your solution be trained, deployed, and scaled to handle tens of 
thousands of LS-NII images per day across multiple scanner types. 
8. Have your products been field tested: 
a. If so, what were the operational settings (vehicle types, environments, throughput)? 
b. What is the scope of commodities and modalities fielded and where? 
c. What is the average volume handled by your solution, in terms of number of images 
processed daily and size of the average image?  
d. What is the Technology Readiness Level?  
e. What are the performance results, including detection and false alarm rates where 
available? 
9. Describe your methods and requirements for training, verification, and deployment: 
a. Do you have your own test data or is government data required? If government data is 
required, what metadata would be required, and what is the minimum metadata you 
can effectively use? 
b. How does your solution perform when metadata is incomplete, inconsistent, or 
inaccurate even provided in the correct format? 
c. Access to CBP systems requires a Background Investigation (BI). Do you or any of 
your employees have a CBP BI? If not, would you be able to test or train at a CBP 
location? 
d. What internal company sources of NII data can be leveraged or made available to the 
government for stream of commerce, threat images, simulated threat images? 
e. Describe how you deal with or have dealt with limited or absent labeling or metadata 
when training and validating your models.  
10. Describe your algorithm system integration approach, including: 
a. File formats and APIs? 
b. Common Integration Platform / Common Viewer integration? 
c. If you have a stand-alone and/or proprietary viewer, what steps can you take to 
integrate or consolidate with CBP’s viewer so that CBP can use its existing tools while 
still leveraging your algorithms?  
d. Are the AI/ML models compatible, or can they be made compatible, with algorithms 
generated by other parties in parallel or cascading operation (e.g., standard data 
structures or schemas for exchanging detections and scores)? 
11. Describe how areas of interest, risk scores, and other model results are displayed to officers 
and how officer feedback is captured, if applicable. 
12. How is your AI/ML engine evolving? 
a. Does the AI/ML model evolve through continuous training? If so, please explain your 
approach to continuous or periodic updates, including governance and safeguards. 

 
5 | P a g e  
 
 
b. What is your approach to monitoring performance over time and detecting model drift 
or degradation? 
13. With respect to the applications above, please indicate: 
a. Which types of contraband or conditions (e.g., narcotics, weapons, generic anomalies, 
modifications, currency, other prohibited or high-risk items) your AI/ML currently 
addresses or has been trained on? 
b. Which LS-NII modalities are supported (e.g., POVs, cargo vehicles, sea containers, 
rail cargo), and what would be required to extend to additional conveyance types if 
needed? 
14. What investment, acquisition, design, and management strategies would be conducive to 
minimizing technical risk and life cycle costs while accelerating development and deployment 
of algorithms into CBP’s existing LS-NII architectures? 
15. How can industry help to standardize and leverage technology and software solutions for use 
across various ports of entry and other facilities to maximize interoperability across systems, 
when feasible, while still allowing CBP to rely on its own data platforms and pipelines? 
16. What subcontract / teaming arrangements, including small / disadvantaged businesses, would 
you put in place to address the full range of stated requirements (algorithm development, 
integration, sustainment, operator support)? 
17. What collaborative activities should government and private sector entities undertake to 
encourage the development and adoption of open architecture, non-proprietary AI/ML 
solutions that can be integrated into diverse LS-NII environments? 
 
4.0 RFI Response Instructions  
 
Only electronic submissions will be accepted. Electronic files larger than 10 MB shall be broken 
down into multiple files with no one file exceeding 10 MB. Each electronic submission shall include:  
 
1. The RFI title in the subject line  
2. The maximum number of pages per submission shall be limited to fifteen (15) pages 
excluding title page, table of contents, company information page and reference materials, if 
attached.  
3. All content must be provided in Microsoft Word or PDF format.  
4. The company information page shall include the following information: 
- Company Name 
- Socio-economic status 
- DUNS number, UEI number, and CAGE code 
- Point-of-Contact information for technical questions 
- Point-of-Contact information for contractual questions 
- Federal Contract(s) available for use 
 
5. The file number and total files being submitted (e.g., File 1 of 4, File 2 of 4, etc.) in the 

 
6 | P a g e  
 
 
subject line, if submission includes more than one electronic email. 
This notice is part of Government Market Research, a continuous process for obtaining the latest 
information on the commercial status of the industry. This RFI is for planning purposes, and does not 
constitute a commitment, implied or otherwise, that a procurement action will follow.  
CBP will use the information submitted in response to this notice at its discretion and will not provide 
comments to any submission; however, CBP reserves the right to contact any respondent to this 
notice for the sole purpose of enhancing CBP's understanding of the notice submission. The

STATEMENT OF WORK (SERVICES)

(SOW)

GENERAL INFORMATION

Rebuilding of TRASIS ALL-IN-ONE

The AllinOne must be restored to the functioning states by repairing/replacing/recalibrating many componenents (actuators and sensors) in order to be used for radiochemical synthesis in hot cell 7. 

NIMH was awarded a used TRASIS AllInone by NCI (Frederick, MD) and the box has not been serviced by anyone for three years. A NIMH chemist, placed AllinOne in Von Gahlen hot cell 7 in room 351. He was able to operate rotary actuators and syringe pumps. However, according to the service engineers, Kaveh, there are many components in the system needs to be recalibarated and repaired to safely and effectively use the AllinOne.  Miuse of the sensitive equipment results in severe damage to the valuable instrument.. There are HPLC injectors, UV detector, two Knauer HPLC pumps needs to be repaired and preventative maintenance service should be performed to operate the equipment properly.

The objective of this rebuilding service is to restore the AllinOne to the usable state where all actuators, and syringe pumps, and UV and radiation detector operate within manufacturer’s specification.

Not applicable

SCOPE OF WORK

The rebuild includes the vacuum and pressure systems, including internal vacuum and pressure lines, valves, check valves, regulators, vacuum pump, vacuum sensor, pressure sensor, and related fittings.

For the HPLC system, the service includes the HPLC pump head rebuild, including pistons, check valves, gaskets/seals, HPLC lines, eluent lines, eluent filters, eluent bottles, HPLC waste lines, priming components, and waste bottles.

All 5 syringe actuators and 30 rotary actuators are inspected, tested, adjusted, and qualified. They are not fully rebuilt unless a specific defective component is found and approved for replacement.

Electronic cards/boards are not included for proactive replacement or rebuild unless a specific electronic fault is identified and separately approved.

Based on the current condition of the unit, we understand that several components required for proper installation are missing. These required installation-package components will be provided as part of this scope.

This quotation is for a 3-year preventive maintenance/rebuild service, installation, qualification, and training. It is not a separate extended service contract unless otherwise specified. However, all parts replaced during this service are covered under a one-year warranty.

Caution: Components that are inspected but not replaced are not covered as replacement parts. Electronic boards/cards, computer hardware, software/security updates, site utilities, external gas supply, contamination, misuse, radiation damage, and customer-maintained consumables are excluded unless specifically included in the quotation or separately approved.

The quotation includes two days of training. The training will cover general system operation, routine user maintenance, basic troubleshooting, review of the serviced and installed components, and review of the qualification results.

The 3-year maintenance and installation service includes:

System installation includes software and missing hardware installation.

Providing the required missing installation-package components currently needed for installation

Pre-maintenance inspection

System cleaning verification

Database backup

CPU settings backup

Statistics/aging data extraction

CPU and power supply checks

Fuses and batteries, as applicable

Five Syringe actuator inspection and qualification

Thirty Rotary actuator inspection, cleaning, and qualification

Replacement of vacuum and pressure internal lines

Replacement/service of check valves and related fittings

Vacuum pump replacement/service

Vacuum and pressure sensor calibration/qualification

Regulator verification/calibration

HPLC pump head rebuild kit installation, including pistons, check valves, gaskets, and seals

Replacement of HPLC lines, eluent lines, filters, eluent bottles, waste lines, and waste bottles

HPLC leak, pressure, flow, priming, and degassing tests

Heater qualification, cooling test, and safety thermoswitch verification

UV detector operational verification

Radioactivity detector response verification, if activity is available

Final maintenance, installation, and qualification report

 

LEVEL OF EFFORT:

Not Applicable

GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITIES

The government scientist should provide the required material for installation. For example, chemicals, tubing, fittings, and utility gas with adequate quality must be provided to the installing engineer in hot cell 7. The government scientist must learn how to operate the machine and how to write the programming scripts. Government scientists will lean also how to properly maintain the AllinOne.

DELIVERY OR DELIVERABLES

REPORTING REQUIREMENTS 

The installation documents such and IQ and OQ shall be provided to the government scientists.

OTHER CONSIDERATIONS

Must be included as part of the pricing.

Title: Radio System Upgrade (RSU) for International Airborne Advance Warning and Control 
System (AWACS)

Product Service Code:  N016 – Installation of Equipme nt / Aircraft Components and 
Accessories 
 
NAICS Code: 541330 – Engineering Services 
 
Notice Type: Notice of Contract Action (NOCA) 
 
 
This notice is from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) AWACS 
and Wedgetail Contracting Office (WIWK) located at 3 Eglin Street, Hanscom Air Force 
Base, Massachusetts 01731.  
 
The previously publicized RSU  NOCA, is intended for final FOPR release within Q2 
CY2026. The FOPR will only be released on the General Services Administration (GSA) 
One Acquisition Solution for Integrated Services Plus (OASIS+) within the Technical and 
Engineering Domain. Interested Bidders should have access to SIPR e -mail in order to 
received classified Technical Documentation needed for submission of complete proposal.  
 
The Government is not requesting any information or proposals in response to this notice. 
 
The Government will be holding a Request for Proposal walk -through at a date and time 
to be set upon release of this solicitation. Bidders interested in attending can look for an 
announcement on GSA OASIS+.

RSU for International AWACS shall include a full upgrade to the Ultra -High Frequency 
(UHF)/Very-High Frequency (VHF) and High-Frequency (HF) radio suite to a full fleet of 
aircraft. Integration and installation of the radios will provide the Second Generation Anti-
Jam Tactical UHF Radio for North America Treaty Organization (NATO) (SATURN) and 
Tactical Secure Voice Cryptographic Interoperability Specification (TSVCIS) capabilities 
for the aircraft.

for small businesses. This notice is not a solicitation, request for quote (RFQ), or request for 
proposal (RFP). The issuance of this RFI and responses thereto do not imply a commitment to 
release a solicitation. A determination by the Government not to compete any or all portions of 
the work discussed in this RFI rests solely within the discretion of the Government. The 
Government will not pay for time, effort, materials, or any other costs that arise as a consequence 
of responding to this RFI. 
The anticipated North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Code is 541611 
(Administrative Management and General Management Consulting Services) with a 
corresponding size standard of $24.5 million. The Product Service Code is anticipated to be 
R499 (Other Professional Services).  
This is a non-commercial acquisition. 
Synopsis 
The Administration for Community Living (ACL), Administration on Disabilities (AoD), Office 
of Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (OIDD), is conducting market research for a 
potential requirement for a Training and Technical Assistance (T/TA) provider to support State 
Councils on Developmental Disabilities (SCDDs). 
Under the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act of 2000 (DD Act), ACL 
supports a nationwide network of 56 State and Territory Councils responsible for advancing 
systems change, advocacy, and capacity building to improve outcomes for individuals with 
intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) and their families.  
The contemplated requirement is for contractor support to deliver coordinated, comprehensive, 
and performance-based T/TA at a national scale, including both foundational and specialized 
support aligned with statutory, governance, and operational requirements of the Councils.  
The effort is intended to strengthen Council capacity to: 
• Maintain compliance with DD Act requirements  
• Implement Five-Year State Plans effectively  

• Demonstrate measurable systems-change outcomes  
• Improve leadership, governance, and evaluation capacity  
• Enhance dissemination, stakeholder engagement, and public awareness  
The Government anticipates a single-award, performance-based contract with a five-year period 
of performance (base + four option years).  
 
The contractor will be required to perform the following tasks: 
1. Project Management and Performance-Based Evaluation 
Provide enterprise-level project management, including development of a Five-Year 
Strategic Plan, monthly and annual reporting, and implementation of performance 
monitoring systems to track outcomes and continuous quality improvement. 
2. Comprehensive Training and Technical Assistance Delivery 
Deliver coordinated T/TA across all 56 Councils, including both foundational and 
specialized support tailored to varying levels of Council capacity and emerging needs. 
3. Knowledge Development and Dissemination 
Develop and disseminate training resources, toolkits, webinars, and national learning 
events, including maintaining a centralized repository of accessible resources. 
4. Leadership, Governance, and Compliance Support 
Provide specialized T/TA on governance structures, leadership development, fiscal 
management, federal reporting, and compliance with DD Act requirements. 
5. Evaluation and Performance Measurement Support 
Support Councils in strengthening evaluation capacity, including development of 
performance indicators, outcome measurement, and application of frameworks such as 
“Trace-the-Line” linking activities to outcomes.  
6. Peer Learning and Network Collaboration 
Facilitate communities of practice, peer exchanges, and cross-state collaboration to 
promote knowledge sharing and systems-level improvement. 
7. Stakeholder Engagement and Systems Change Support 
Support Councils in engaging individuals with I/DD, families, and partners to advance 
advocacy, inclusion, and systems change outcomes. 

8. Information Management and Technology Support 
Develop and maintain a secure, Section 508-compliant website and performance 
dashboard to support resource dissemination, performance tracking, and stakeholder 
engagement.  
9. Communications and Public Awareness 
Provide T/TA to enhance dissemination strategies, public awareness, and communication 
of Council roles, activities, and outcomes. 
10. Transition Support 
Provide transition-in and transition-out support to ensure continuity of services and 
minimal disruption to Council operations. 
Note: The anticipated place of performance is primarily remote at the contractor’s site. 
 
Response 
Interested vendors should address their capability and experience in the following areas: 
1. Delivery of large-scale, national T/TA programs across distributed networks  
2. Experience with Developmental Disabilities Act programs or similar federal disability 
initiatives  
3. Enterprise-level project management and performance-based service delivery  
4. Development of training resources, toolkits, and knowledge dissemination platforms  
5. Leadership development, governance, and compliance support  
6. Evaluation design, performance measurement, and outcome reporting  
7. Facilitation of peer learning, communities of practice, and stakeholder engagement  
8. Development of Section 508-compliant materials and accessible digital content  
9. Design and implementation of performance dashboards and reporting systems  
10. Experience managing high-volume, concurrent activities across multiple jurisdictions  
11. Transition planning and knowledge transfer capabilities  
 
The following shall be addressed in your submission:

As stated above, this request is issued solely for Information and Planning Purposes. It does not

The Government requests that no proprietary or confidential business information be submitted. 
Responses will be used for planning purposes only and will not be returned. The Government is 
under no obligation to provide feedback or acknowledge receipt of responses.  
This requirement is currently considered non-commercial. Interested parties are requested to 
indicate whether they believe the requirement could be fulfilled using commercial services, as 
defined in FAR Part 2.101, and, if so, provide a detailed rationale supporting that determination. 
Please respond by email Kaitlin White at Kaitlin.White@hhs.gov by 9:00 AM ET on May 8, 
2026, with your response to the areas of expertise above. Please reference Notice ID 
Training_and_TA. No extensions will be granted.

REQUEST FOR INFORMATION (RFI) FOR DESCRIPTION FOR SERVICES
Purpose-Built Attritable Systems (PBAS)
Bomber Family of Systems Expansion

1. INTRODUCTION

The U.S. Army Contracting Command – Aberdeen Proving Ground (ACC-APG) is issuing this Request for Information (RFI) to conduct market research and assess industry capability and technology maturity to support the Purpose-Built Attritable Systems (PBAS) program.

PBAS is focused on delivering small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (sUAS) capable of employing lethal and non-lethal effects at the lowest tactical level. The Government is interested in expanding the scope of PBAS to include a family of systems, incorporating both small and larger air vehicles capable of conducting One-Way-Attack (OWA), droppable munition delivery, Reconnaissance, Surveillance, and Target Acquisition (RSTA) and marsupial operations.  The larger variants are commonly referred to as bombers or bombardier.

This RFI seeks information from industry on existing or emerging capabilities that support these mission sets.

The U.S. Government may use the results of this market research to inform future solicitations under authorities including, but not limited to, 10 U.S.C. §4022 (Other Transaction Authority) and 10 U.S.C. §4023 (Procurement for Experimental Purposes). Multiple award strategies may be considered.

This RFI is for informational purposes only and does not constitute a solicitation.

2. PROGRAM BACKGROUND

The employment of Small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (sUAS) provides maneuver leaders increased situational awareness and extends the range of both lethal and non-lethal effects at the tactical edge.

Current ISR/RSTA-focused sUAS lack the ability to:
- Provide scalable, low-cost, and attritable strike capability  that delivers to the operational force necessary organic Hunter-Killer capability at scale

PBAS addresses this gap by enabling:
- Droppable and integrated lethality  
- Improved maneuverability and concealability  
- Low-cost, scalable employment at the platoon level and below  

The Government is looking to expand PBAS to include larger bomber-class air vehicles capable of extending range, payload capacity, and mission flexibility.

3. REQUIRED CAPABILITY

The U.S. Army has an immediate need for PBAS to integrate droppable lethality into air vehicles to achieve and maintain overmatch capability. Common Lethality Integration Kit (CLIK) or Mallet interface compliance is desired.  

Mallet is a fuze conversion kit that enables existing munitions to be safely and effectively employed as sUAS-delivered drop munitions without modifying the original munition.  It is the munitions adapter/fuze layer that enables legacy munitions for drone-delivered effects.

Desired engagement capabilities include:

Personnel targets – Effects intended to incapacitate or eliminate individual or grouped personnel.

Light to medium materiel targets – Effects designed to damage or disable equipment such as unarmored or lightly armored vehicles, sensors, and infrastructure.

Neutralization, obscuration, and deception effects – Effects that degrade enemy capability by suppressing activity, limiting visibility and preventing or delaying enemy movement.

Hardened structures – Effects capable of penetrating, damaging, or destroying fortified or reinforced positions such as bunkers or hardened facilities.

Multiple (2 or more) munitions are desired for payload capacity. Munition examples include, but are not limited to:

60mm mortars

81mm mortars

MK118 cluster munitions

M67 Grenade

Air vehicles shall demonstrate the ability to:

Deploy droppable munitions against enemy targets during night/low-light conditions in addition to thermal capability

Maintain stable flight during payload release  

Cost of platform is meant to be attritable. This platform will drop payloads and return-to-home, but the useful life of the platform in an operating environment will be low (measured in no more than 20 successful mission). Due to low cost and high performance, the system will allow soldiers to take on more risk with employment, and the program office will be able to replenish systems affordably. 

Return to the operator or designated recovery point for reloading and re-employment

Have a damaged airframe repaired forward by Soldiers with readily available components, rapidly designed and printed repair parts, while forward in the field, and returned to operators with minimal downtime.

The ability to process and share the video and/or metadata output in an open format, without vendor permission or proprietary tooling.


Air vehicles within Group 1 and Group 2 categories (up to 55 lbs.) are desired. Group 3 (greater than 55 lbs,) or larger systems should not be submitted. The weight classification specifically refers to the Maximum Gross Takeoff Weight (MGTOW), which includes the weight of the air vehicle, its fuel, and its payload.

4. ADDITIONAL REQUIRED CAPABILITY – BOMBER FAMILY OF SYSTEMS

The Government is specifically interested in industry capabilities that support expansion of PBAS into a family of systems, to include larger “bomber” variants.

Respondents should address one or more of the following mission areas:

a. Droppable Munition Delivery  
Air vehicles capable of carrying and deploying one or more droppable munitions against designated targets.

b. Reusable Strike Capability  
Ability to conduct munition delivery and return for rapid reloading and re-employment.

c. Marsupial Operations  
Air vehicles capable of carrying and deploying smaller UAS (e.g., 5-inch class systems) to extend operational reach and enable distributed effects.

d. RSTA Integration
Persistent RSTA capability to support target identification, tracking, and battle damage assessment (BDA).

e. Aiming and targeting software to reduce cognitive load on soldiers and assist in executing targets.

5. SYSTEM ATTRIBUTES AND CONSTRAINTS

Respondents should address system performance against the following parameters:

Maximum System Weight: The weight classification specifically refers to the Maximum Gross Takeoff Weight (MGTOW), which includes the weight of the air vehicle and its payload(s).

Operational Range: Desired range of 20–40 km  

System Classes of Interest:

Group 1 / Group 2 bomber-class systems  

Payload Modularity: Systems should support modular payload integration (e.g., CLIK and Mallet or equivalent MOSA approach)

Autonomy & Control:

Operator-in-the-loop or supervised autonomy  

Waypoint navigation and return-to-home capability  

Operation in contested/degraded environments preferred

MOSA compliant avionics

The capacity to run ATR day and night and to update ATR models, including using 3rd part models, according to mission needs 

6. AREAS OF INTEREST FOR INDUSTRY RESPONSE

Respondents are encouraged to provide description of:

Existing or prototype bomber-style sUAS platforms  

Payload capacity and types/quantity of droppable munitions supported  

Marsupial capabilities (deployment of smaller UAS)  

Target acquisition and aiming software (payload on platform and on shooter’s GCS)

RSTA payload capabilities and sensor integration  

Demonstrated range, endurance, and mission profiles  

Launch methods (Eg. Rails, catapult, launch tube, Vertical Take-Off and Landing, Conventional Take Off and Landing)

Recovery methods (Eg. Vertical Take-Off and Landing, Conventional Take Off and Landing)

Interface approach (CLIK/MALLET) or other MOSA-compliant solution)  

Manufacturing readiness and scalability

Price

100 complete systems

1000 complete systems

10000 complete systems

MOSA architecture

NDAA/DCMA Compliance.  If not compliant, current plan to achieve requirement.

Bill of Materials (BOM) with prices

7. ELIGIBILITY

The applicable NAICS code for this requirement is 541715 with a Small Business Size Standard of 1,000 employees. The Product Service Code is AJ11.

Businesses of all sizes are encouraged to respond. Respondents must clearly identify their business size in their submission. Also include, if applicable, the company’s status as a Nontraditional Defense Contractor, as defined at 10 U.S.C. 3014 and in compliance with updated thresholds in Section 1806 of 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). 

8. SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Interested parties shall submit a capabilities statement that:

- Is no more than 20 pages (8.5 x 11)  
- Uses font no smaller than 10-point  
- May include images, diagrams, or system descriptions  

Submissions shall include:

- Organization name and address  
- Technical point of contact  
- Phone number and email address  
- CAGE Code and UEI  
- Business size and ownership type

9. SUBMISSION DEADLINE

Responses are due no later than 1000 EDT on 22 May 2026

All responses shall be submitted via email to the designated Government points of contact.

No phone calls will be accepted.

10. QUESTIONS

All questions must be submitted via email to the points of contact listed above.

The Government is not obligated to respond to inquiries or provide feedback on submissions.

11. DISCLAIMER

This RFI is issued for informational purposes only and does not constitute a Request for Proposal (RFP).

- This is not a solicitation  
- The Government is not obligated to award a contract  
- No funds are available for response preparation  
- All submissions are voluntary

FAR Subpart 3.11  Preventing Personal Conflicts of Interest for Contractor Employees Performing Acquisition Functions 

In accordance with these provisions, contractor employees performing certain acquisition-related functions for the Government (a) must disclose and avoid/prevent personal conflicts of interest and the appearance thereof, and (b) may not use or disclose for personal gain any non-public information to which they have access by reason of performance on a Government contract.

A Personal Conflict of Interest is a situation in which a covered contractor employee has a financial interest, personal activity or relationship that could impair his or her ability to act impartially and in the best interest of the Government when performing under a contract. For example, the contractor employee, or a person whose financial interests are imputed to him/her, may have a financial interest -- through investments, prospective employment or business, or gifts – in the prime or in a subcontractor involved in an acquisition in which the contractor employee is providing an Acquisition Function. Sources of Personal Conflicts of Interest include:

Financial interests of the contractor employee, close family members or other members of his or her  household;

Other employment or financial relationships (including seeking or negotiation for prospective employment or business; and

Gifts (including travel).

FAR Subpart 37.104  Personal Services Contracts

This provision stipulates that a personal services contract is characterized by the employer-employee relationship it creates between the Government and the contractor’s personnel.  The awarded contract identified above is for support services to assist ONR in accomplishment of the mission and is not a personal services contract.

The full text of this clause can be found at:  http://farsite.hill.af.mil/reghtml/regs/far2afmcfars/fardfars/far/37.htm#P52_7302
